claims.text: The coating is a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy with an established interphase-boundary network.
Creep resistance is chiefly controlled by the density and character of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
Pinning at interphase boundaries impedes dislocation motion during sustained loading.
Impeded dislocation motion limits progressive plastic deformation.
Controlled heat treatment or modified processing can be used to vary the coating's interphase-boundary density.
Boundary pinning forces deformation toward less efficient mechanisms such as dislocation climb or diffusion creep.
The shift toward dislocation climb or diffusion creep slows the rate of plastic deformation.
Samples with higher interphase-boundary density will have a lower creep strain rate than samples with lower boundary density or a more continuous phase structure.
Samples with higher interphase-boundary density will accumulate less overall plastic deformation over time.
The proposed mechanism governs creep only where dislocation-based plasticity is prevalent.
The proposed mechanism requires the dual-phase microstructure to remain stable during sustained loading.
General materials principles support a role for interphase boundaries in hindering dislocation motion.
The relative importance of interphase-boundary effects versus solute effects and grain-boundary strengthening in the specific alloy is not quantitatively established.
